lines.text: Coral atolls scattered across the Pacific, home to master navigators, then to empires and the bombs of the atomic age. This is the story of the Marshall Islands.
Marshallese sailors crossed the open ocean with charts made of sticks and shells, mapping the swells that ran between their islands.
In 1885, Germany took the Marshalls into its colony of German New Guinea. After the First World War, Japan ruled them.
Amata Kabua, born in 1928, would grow up to become the first president of the islands.
In 1944, American forces stormed Kwajalein atoll, and the islands passed from Japan into American hands.
In 1946, the islanders of Bikini were moved away, and the United States set off its first atomic tests in the lagoon.
That same summer, a daring two-piece swimsuit appeared in France, named after the atoll that had just made headlines.
From 1947, the United States ran the islands as a United Nations trust territory.
Hilda Heine, born in 1951, would become president, the first woman to lead a Pacific island country.
In 1954, Castle Bravo, the largest American hydrogen bomb ever tested, exploded at Bikini, and its fallout poisoned nearby atolls.
In time a Compact of Free Association was agreed with the United States, coming into force in 1986.
By 1980, a great concrete dome had been laid on Runit island at Enewetak, sealing in radioactive waste from the tests.
And in 1986, the Marshall Islands became a self-governing nation, freely associated with the United States.
From stick charts to a nation of their own, the Marshallese still carry the memory of the tests.
